3	\subsection{Experimental Setup}\label{sec:setup}
4	
5	\paragraph{Datasets.}
6	We evaluate on four English NER benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
7	\textbf{SciERC} \cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test instances, 6 entity types) is the primary medium-difficulty test bed (${\approx}$65\% F1).
8	\textbf{Few-NERD} \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (INTRA coarse; 37{,}648 instances, 8 entity types, ${\approx}$75\% F1) provides a low-degeneracy contrast where LP selection succeeds (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}).
9	\textbf{CoNLL-2003} \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (3{,}453 test sentences, 4 entity types, ${\approx}$91\% F1) serves as a ceiling-effect control.
10	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (1{,}287 social media instances, 51\% zero F1) probes the signal-collapse boundary.
11	
12	\paragraph{Models and sampling.}
13	\textbf{Qwen3-8B} and \textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} are LoRA fine-tuned using LLaMA Factory \cite{zheng2024llamafactory} (Appendix~\ref{app:training}; Few-NERD uses 3 epochs vs.\ 5 for others; Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).
14	$N{=}8$ samples at $T{=}1.0$ (primary) with vLLM constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}; $N{=}16$ for scaling (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).

1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	NER exhibits oracle scaling ($c{\approx}0.5$; \S\ref{sec:scaling}), but degeneracy (12.2--67.9\%) and LP-quality alignment ($\rho$ 0.043--0.667) constrain aggregation; temperature disentangles these at $T{=}1.2$ (Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}).
4	
5	\paragraph{Degeneracy correlates with the selection gap across model families.}
6	Across four frontier models on Few-NERD, degeneracy and the selection gap (oracle${-}$MV) are negatively correlated (5.5--74\% degen $\to$ 0.290--0.032 gap; Table~\ref{tab:frontier_sc_cross}), consistent with the degeneracy bound (\S\ref{sec:theory}) being structural rather than model-specific.
7	
8	\paragraph{From diagnosis to practice.}\label{sec:selection_method}
9	Entity-level construction bypasses both failure mechanisms, with gains when degeneracy ${<}22$\% and absent when ${>}31$\% ($p{<}0.01$; Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}); no alternative strategy beats greedy (Appendix~\ref{app:dals}, \ref{app:supervised_combination}), making construction the only consistently positive approach (Table~\ref{tab:cost_benefit})---though the trade-off ($N{\times}$ cost for ${\approx}1$\,pp) may only justify safety-critical use.
10	LP compression (median 0.041 nats) connects to calibration challenges \cite{kadavath2022language, xiong2024verbalized}; per-sample alternatives \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} remain untested.

## α_crit Entity Selection Bound (v4 — Unified Strict MV)

> **v3→v4 change**: MV threshold unified from inclusive `≥ N/2 = 4` to strict `> N/2` (N=8: need ≥5/8 votes).
> Entity match: 4-tuple (text, type, start, end). Data source: MF4v2 pipeline samples.jsonl.
> Evaluation: gold-non-empty instances only, micro-F1 (aggregate TP/FP/FN).

### Main Table (T=1.0, MF4v2 micro-F1, strict MV > N/2)

| Dataset | Seeds | greedy_f1 | mv_f1 | oracle_f1 | Δ_SC (pp) | α_crit | δ (degen) | α_crit_eff | δ > 1−α_crit? |
|---------|-------|-----------|-------|-----------|-----------|--------|-----------|------------|---------------|
| FewNERD | 3 (42/123/456) | 0.7912 | 0.7638 | 0.8852 | **−2.74±0.54** | 0.3956 | 8.8% | 0.4338 | No (8.8% < 60.4%) |
| CoNLL   | 3 (42/123/456) | 0.9119 | 0.9115 | 0.9527 | **−0.04±0.15** | 0.4560 | 60.3% | 1.148 | **Yes** (60.3% > 54.4%) |
| SciERC  | 3 (42/123/456) | 0.6670 | 0.6596 | 0.7808 | **−0.74±0.57** | 0.3335 | 12.2% | 0.3799 | No (12.2% < 66.7%) |

- **Δ_SC** = mv_f1 − greedy_f1. All three datasets: MV **loses** to greedy under strict threshold.
- **α_crit** = F₁^gr / 2 (Proposition 1: marginal-entity precision threshold for Δ F₁ > 0)
- **α_crit_eff** = α_crit / (1 − δ). CoNLL α_crit_eff > 1.0 means MV gain structurally impossible given degeneracy.
- **δ**: fraction of gold-non-empty instances where all N=8 samples produce identical entity sets.
- ⚠️ **v4 公式修正**: 旧版脚本用 `π_MV/(2−π_MV)` 计算 α_crit（错误），已改为 Proposition 1 的 `F₁^gr/2`。

### Per-Seed Detail

#### FewNERD (n=32,565 gold-non-empty instances per seed)

| Seed | greedy_f1 | mv_f1 | oracle_f1 | degen | α_crit | Δ_SC (pp) |
|------|-----------|-------|-----------|-------|--------|-----------|
| 42   | 0.7913 | 0.7580 | 0.8803 | 9.1% | 0.3957 | −3.33 |
| 123  | 0.7908 | 0.7645 | 0.8899 | 9.2% | 0.3954 | −2.63 |
| 456  | 0.7915 | 0.7689 | 0.8855 | 8.1% | 0.3958 | −2.27 |

#### CoNLL (n=2,756 gold-non-empty instances per seed)

| Seed | greedy_f1 | mv_f1 | oracle_f1 | degen | α_crit | Δ_SC (pp) |
|------|-----------|-------|-----------|-------|--------|-----------|
| 42   | 0.9123 | 0.9101 | 0.9538 | 60.1% | 0.4562 | −0.22 |
| 123  | 0.9119 | 0.9123 | 0.9542 | 60.3% | 0.4560 | +0.04 |
| 456  | 0.9116 | 0.9121 | 0.9502 | 60.4% | 0.4558 | +0.05 |

#### SciERC (n=529 gold-non-empty instances per seed)

| Seed | greedy_f1 | mv_f1 | oracle_f1 | degen | α_crit | Δ_SC (pp) |
|------|-----------|-------|-----------|-------|--------|-----------|
| 42   | 0.6683 | 0.6558 | 0.7840 | 13.4% | 0.3342 | −1.24 |
| 123  | 0.6663 | 0.6652 | 0.7789 | 11.0% | 0.3332 | −0.11 |
| 456  | 0.6663 | 0.6577 | 0.7795 | 12.1% | 0.3332 | −0.86 |

### v3 → v4 Delta (threshold change: ≥4/8 → ≥5/8)

Impact on mv_f1 (greedy/oracle/δ unchanged since they don't depend on MV threshold):

| Dataset | Seed | mv_f1 (v3 incl) | mv_f1 (v4 strict) | Δ mv_f1 (pp) |
|---------|------|------------------|--------------------|--------------|
| FewNERD | 42   | 0.7777 | 0.7580 | −1.97 |
| FewNERD | 123  | 0.7845 | 0.7645 | −2.00 |
| FewNERD | 456  | 0.7857 | 0.7689 | −1.68 |
| CoNLL   | 42   | 0.9128 | 0.9101 | −0.27 |
| CoNLL   | 123  | 0.9151 | 0.9123 | −0.28 |
| CoNLL   | 456  | 0.9133 | 0.9121 | −0.12 |
| SciERC  | 42   | 0.6640 | 0.6558 | −0.82 |
| SciERC  | 123  | 0.6689 | 0.6652 | −0.37 |
| SciERC  | 456  | 0.6687 | 0.6577 | −1.10 |

Note: α_crit = F₁^gr/2 不随 MV 阈值变化（仅取决于 greedy_f1），故不再列对比。

**Strict threshold consistently lowers mv_f1** by 0.1–2.0pp (largest on FewNERD, smallest on CoNLL s456 at −0.12pp).

| CoNLL | 42 | mv_f1 | 0.9090 | 0.9101 | +0.11pp | data+threshold |

1828	\section{Epoch Confound Analysis}\label{app:epoch_confound}
1829	
1830	\paragraph{Training convergence modulates degeneracy.}
1831	Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound} compares the 3-epoch model (used throughout the main text) with a 5-epoch variant on Few-NERD (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
1832	Extended training increases greedy F1 by $+2.95$~pp (0.748 $\to$ 0.777) but nearly triples instance degeneracy (11.1\% $\to$ 31.3\%), reducing the fraction of instances with non-degenerate outputs from 85.6\% to 68.7\%.
1833	LP selection gains drop correspondingly ($+1.37$~pp $\to$ $+0.62$~pp), consistent with the degeneracy-gating mechanism identified in the main text (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
1834	Within-instance LP-quality alignment is relatively stable under this convergence shift (mean $\rho$: $0.524 \to 0.407$; median $\rho$: $0.667 \to 0.615$), consistent with alignment being determined primarily by task structure rather than training duration.
1835	
1836	Evaluation loss increases after epoch 3 (0.032 $\to$ 0.041 at epoch 5), and the best checkpoint by validation loss occurs at step 32{,}000 (approximately epoch 3.9).
1837	Standard early stopping practice thus naturally selects the low-degeneracy regime where LP selection is most effective.
1838	This finding refines the narrative: degeneracy is not a fixed property of datasets but is modulated by the degree of training convergence. Over-trained models compress their output distributions, collapsing diversity even on datasets that support it under well-regularized training.

\section{Epoch Confound Analysis}\label{app:epoch_confound}

\paragraph{Training convergence modulates degeneracy.}
Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound} compares the 3-epoch model (used throughout the main text) with a 5-epoch variant on Few-NERD (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
Extended training increases greedy F1 by $+2.95$~pp (0.748 $\to$ 0.777) but nearly triples instance degeneracy (11.1\% $\to$ 31.3\%), reducing the fraction of instances with non-degenerate outputs from 85.6\% to 68.7\%.
LP selection gains drop correspondingly ($+1.37$~pp $\to$ $+0.62$~pp), consistent with the degeneracy-gating mechanism identified in the main text (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Within-instance LP-quality alignment is relatively stable under this convergence shift (mean $\rho$: $0.524 \to 0.407$; median $\rho$: $0.667 \to 0.615$), consistent with alignment being determined primarily by task structure rather than training duration.

Evaluation loss increases after epoch 3 (0.032 $\to$ 0.041 at epoch 5), and the best checkpoint by validation loss occurs at step 32{,}000 (approximately epoch 3.9).
Standard early stopping practice thus naturally selects the low-degeneracy regime where LP selection is most effective.
This finding refines the narrative: degeneracy is not a fixed property of datasets but is modulated by the degree of training convergence. Over-trained models compress their output distributions, collapsing diversity even on datasets that support it under well-regularized training.

\paragraph{SciERC epoch curve.}
Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc} extends the analysis to SciERC with a 3-point curve (3, 5, 10 epochs; Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
Degeneracy increases monotonically (6.4\% $\to$ 17.8\% $\to$ 47.8\%), and within-instance LP-quality correlation degrades in tandem (median $\rho$: 0.319 $\to$ 0.262 $\to$ 0.112; mean $\rho$: 0.273 $\to$ 0.179 $\to$ 0.066), confirming that overtraining erodes both diversity and LP alignment simultaneously.
The fraction of instances with positive LP-quality correlation also declines (76.4\% at 3 epochs $\to$ 64.1\% at 5 epochs $\to$ 54.0\% at 10 epochs).
LP selection does not yield significant gains at any training duration ($-1.24$, $+0.64$, $+1.02$~pp; all below the ${\approx}$1.5~pp MDE), despite oracle headroom ranging from 8.4 to 15.0~pp.
The 3-epoch model has higher within-instance alignment ($\rho{=}0.319$) than the 5-epoch model ($\rho{=}0.262$), yet LP selection is worse ($-1.24$ vs.\ $+0.64$~pp): at 6.4\% degeneracy, more non-degenerate instances enter the candidate pool, but LP ranking precision is too low to exploit them, so the broader pool hurts rather than helps. This illustrates that low degeneracy does not ensure selection gains; LP-quality alignment predicts selection direction.
At 10 epochs, the model retains competitive greedy F1 (0.649 vs.\ 0.650 at 3 epochs) yet conditions are unfavorable: 47.8\% degenerate instances and $\rho{=}0.112$.
The gradient confirms that degeneracy is convergence-driven rather than a fixed dataset property: extended training compresses output distributions, degrading both diversity and within-instance alignment. However, the epoch-to-epoch alignment variation ($\Delta\rho_{\text{median}}{=}0.057$) is small relative to the cross-dataset gap (SciERC ${\sim}$0.3 vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5), consistent with alignment being primarily dataset-intrinsic: training convergence modulates alignment at the margin but cannot shift a dataset into the strong-alignment regime.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
The Few-NERD epoch analysis covers 2 points (3 vs.\ 5 epochs); the SciERC curve provides a 3-point gradient showing monotonic degeneracy increase with simultaneous within-instance alignment degradation.
CoNLL epoch variation remains unverified; high-degeneracy datasets (CoNLL at 59--89\%) may exhibit a ceiling effect where additional training has limited marginal impact.
All Few-NERD results in the main text use the 3-epoch model (standard early stopping); the 5-epoch comparison is a controlled ablation.
All SciERC results use the 5-epoch model; the 3- and 10-epoch variants serve as controlled ablations.

\subsection{Degeneracy-Aware LP Selection}\label{app:dals}

The non-tied subset analysis (Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}) identifies within-instance LP range (max minus min LP across $N$ samples) as a per-instance degeneracy proxy: instances with near-zero LP range carry no discriminative signal.
Degeneracy-aware LP selection (DALS) operationalizes this: when LP range exceeds $\tau{=}0.05$ (the threshold independently motivated by the non-tied analysis; Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}), select the highest-LP sample; otherwise fall back to greedy.
On SciERC, DALS yields $+0.71{\pm}0.48$~pp (3-seed mean; individual seeds: $+0.19$ to $+1.14$~pp); on Few-NERD, $+0.30$~pp ($p{<}0.001$; gain remains positive across $\tau \in [0.01, 0.15]$); on CoNLL, where pure LP selection degrades F1 ($-0.85$~pp), DALS shows comparable degradation (Qwen: $-0.87$~pp; LLaMA: neutral).
DALS improves over pure LP selection when degeneracy is moderate, provides partial damage control when LP selection is harmful, and defaults to greedy when LP range signals no information.
While gains are modest and seed-sensitive, LP range serves as an operationally accessible degeneracy proxy, though the mixed cross-dataset results confirm that degeneracy gating alone cannot ensure positive selection outcomes.

\paragraph{LOO $\tau$ sensitivity.}
Leave-one-out (LOO) cross-validation across datasets shows that the optimal $\tau$ spans two orders of magnitude: $\tau^*{=}0.001$ on Few-NERD, $0.05$ on SciERC, and $0.10$ on CoNLL.

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Test-time compute scaling complements model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling}: repeated sampling with majority voting \cite{wang2023selfconsistency}, best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, brown2024monkeys}, and extended chain-of-thought \cite{muennighoff2025s1} produce large gains on reasoning and code generation.
These successes share a structural prerequisite: the output space admits either exact equivalence classes (multiple-choice, numeric answers) or execution-based verification (code).
Named entity recognition (NER) breaks both assumptions.
The output is a set of typed entities; two samples from the same input routinely extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and no external oracle can adjudicate correctness at test time.
Without equivalence classes, majority voting reduces to heuristic frequency counting; without a verifier, best-of-$N$ requires a reliable proxy signal.
This structural mismatch raises a concrete question: can self-consistency signals that estimate quality well for reasoning tasks also \textit{select} better outputs or \textit{construct} better entity sets for NER?
We investigate this question for NER and extend exploratorily to SQL parsing, treating NER as a representative instance of the broader set-valued generation problem.

The question has practical stakes beyond information extraction.
Hallucination detection methods such as SelfCheckGPT \cite{manakul2023selfcheckgpt} and FActScore \cite{min2023factscore} rely on cross-sample consistency to verify individual claims: if a model's outputs agree, the shared content is presumed factual.
This reasoning assumes entity-level self-verification works, that a model can reliably distinguish correct extractions from incorrect ones through self-judgment or re-prompting.
We show this assumption fails.
Three independent probes (entity self-judgment, multi-round re-prompting, latent-space aggregation) all yield chance-level or negative results for a fine-tuned 8B model on NER.
Recent work \cite{yao2026consistency} demonstrates that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy across benchmarks but does not diagnose \textit{when} or \textit{why} this correlation breaks down at the selection level.
Our diagnostic framework addresses this question: four failure modes (degeneracy, low agreement, false agreement, LP compression) characterize how strong instance-level correlation coexists with negligible sample-level selection gain.

We call this disparity the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Five quality estimation (QE) signals achieve rank correlations up to $\rho{=}0.45$ and AUROC up to 0.82 with oracle F1, yet no signal outperforms greedy decoding on SciERC (all $p{\geq}0.29$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
Only log-probability (LP) achieves a positive selection gain, and only on Few-NERD ($+1.39$\,pp; Holm $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.021$, selection family $k{=}21$).
To test whether entity-level methods can close this gap, we evaluated nine method categories spanning prompt-based self-verification, latent-space aggregation, and supervised classifiers (Table~\ref{tab:method_summary}).
No method produces statistically significant F1 improvement over majority vote on any tested configuration across three NER datasets and two model families (Appendix~\ref{app:method_coverage}).
A supervised hidden-state probe achieves entity-level AUROC${=}0.63$\textendash$0.88$ from a single forward pass, exceeding prompt-based self-judgment (${=}0.51$) but not uniformly exceeding multi-sample agreement (${=}0.87$)---an introspection boundary modulated by task complexity (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}).

These findings rest on controlled experiments across four NER benchmarks (SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc}, Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd}, CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll}, WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut}), two model families (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), 4B/14B ablations, and sample sizes $N {\in} \{2, \ldots, 32\}$.
We extend to Qwen2.5-72B and GPT-5.5 zero-shot to confirm the ceiling is not model-family-specific (\S\ref{sec:scaling}), and extend exploratorily to RE (55.5\% zero-F1 instances;\footnote{RE F1 is confounded by entity span errors: the majority of zero-F1 RE instances reflect upstream NER mismatches rather than relation classification failure (Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).} \S\ref{sec:discussion}) and SQL parsing (87.2\% degeneracy).

\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap (diagnostic sequence, not causal chain; Qwen3-8B fine-tuned, Few-NERD, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). \textbf{Left}: consistency signals estimate instance quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates, so selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: LP-weighted entity construction ($\theta{=}2/N$) bypasses the bottleneck ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

    \item \textbf{Diagnostic framework.}
    A reusable four-stage diagnostic protocol (QE $\to$ degeneracy $\to$ agreement fidelity $\to$ LP compression) characterizing where and how self-consistency fails for NER (\S\ref{sec:selection_gap}, \S\ref{sec:discussion}).

    \item \textbf{Self-verification ceiling.}
    Nine method categories across three NER datasets and two model families all fail to close the correlation-selection gap (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}, \S\ref{sec:adaptive}).

    \item \textbf{Introspection gap.}
    A supervised probe achieves entity-level AUROC${=}0.63$\textendash$0.88$ (GroupKFold CV), exceeding self-judgment (${=}0.51$) but falling below multi-sample agreement (${=}0.87$) on two of three datasets---hidden states encode partial entity quality inaccessible through prompting (\S\ref{sec:mechanistic}).

    \item \textbf{Prescriptive escape routes.}
    Entity-level construction ($+0.32$\,--\,$1.40$\,pp), cross-model ensemble ($+0.42$\,pp), and regime-specific LP selection ($+1.39$\,pp) bypass sample-level selection by operating at entity granularity; a degeneracy threshold $\theta_{\text{crit}}{=}0.70$ predicts when gains vanish (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}, \S\ref{sec:theory}).
